This is a great observation and a real problem called LLM over-generosity.

Why the LLM Gave 8/10 Despite No Match

The LLM is being too lenient because your prompt is not strict enough:


python
# ❌ Your current prompt — too vague
f"Score this resume from 0 to 10 based on clarity, specificity 
and relevance to the job description."

The LLM reads the JD which says:

"diverse academic backgrounds are encouraged"
"strong analytical thinking"
"eager to learn"
"adaptable"

And then thinks — "this candidate knows Python, has projects, shows problem-solving... that's analytical thinking! 8/10!"

The LLM is not lying — it's just being generous with vague criteria.

The Fix — Make the Prompt Strict and Specific

python
def resume_score(state: Hire) -> Hire:
    print("Evaluating the resume and scoring them...")
    structured_llm = llm.with_structured_output(ResumeScore)
    result = structured_llm.invoke(
        f"You are a strict technical recruiter. Score this resume against the job description.\n\n"
        f"Scoring rules:\n"
        f"- If the candidate's core skills do NOT match the JD domain, score must be 0 to 3\n"
        f"- If there is partial match in skills or transferable skills, score 4 to 6\n"
        f"- Only score 7 to 10 if the candidate directly matches the required skills and domain\n"
        f"- Be strict. Do NOT reward general skills like communication or eagerness to learn\n"
        f"- A web developer applying for a cybersecurity role must score below 4\n\n"
        f"Job Description:\n{state.job_description}\n\n"
        f"Resume:\n{state.application}"
    )
    print(f"Resume Score : {result.score}/10")
    return {"resume_score": result.score}
Also Add a skill_match Field to Your State

No explanation	Only score returned	Add reason field to structured output

is using "RAG" for this complete idea =>{building an AI based review system}which i am trying to build is a better approach than "LLM ->AI based review "?

Great question! Let's break this down clearly.

What You're Building vs What RAG Is

What you're building:


Resume PDF → LLM evaluates → Score → Email

The LLM reads the resume and reasons about it directly.

What RAG is:


Large document database → Retrieve relevant chunks → LLM answers based on retrieved chunks
What is RAG Actually?

RAG stands for Retrieval Augmented Generation. It was built to solve one specific problem:

"The LLM doesn't know something — so let's retrieve that information first, then feed it to the LLM"

Classic RAG use case:


Company has 10,000 internal PDF documents
User asks: "What is our refund policy for orders above ₹5000?"
        ↓
RAG searches the 10,000 docs
        ↓
Finds the 3 most relevant paragraphs
        ↓
Feeds those paragraphs to LLM
        ↓
LLM answers accurately

RAG solves the problem of the LLM not having access to your private data.

Is RAG Better for Your Recruiting System?

No — and here's exactly why:

	Your Current Approach	RAG Approach
Input	One resume at a time	Needs a database of documents
LLM reads	The full resume directly	Only retrieved chunks of documents
Best for	Evaluating + reasoning about a single document	Searching across thousands of documents
Your use case fits?	✅ Perfect fit	❌ Overkill
Where RAG Would Actually Help You

RAG becomes useful only if your recruiting system grows into these scenarios:

Scenario 1 — Searching past candidates:


Recruiter asks: "Show me all candidates who know PyTorch 
                 and scored above 7 last month"
        ↓
RAG searches your stored resume database
        ↓
Returns matching candidates

Scenario 2 — Company knowledge base:


Recruiter asks: "Does this candidate match our 
                 internal ML team skill requirements?"
        ↓
RAG retrieves your internal team docs + skill matrices
        ↓
LLM compares candidate against your internal standards

Scenario 3 — Hundreds of JDs:


Company has 200 open roles
System needs to match each resume to the most relevant JD
        ↓
RAG finds the best matching JD from your database
        ↓
LLM scores against that specific JD
The Honest Comparison

YOUR CURRENT SYSTEM
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Resume → LLM → Score → Email

✅ Perfect for what you need right now
✅ Simple, fast, accurate
✅ No extra infrastructure needed
✅ LLM reads the FULL resume — nothing missed
✅ Already production-ready logic


RAG SYSTEM
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Resume → Split into chunks → Store in vector DB
       → Retrieve relevant chunks → LLM → Score

❌ Adds complexity for no benefit here
❌ Chunking a resume loses context
   (LLM might miss key skills split across chunks)
❌ Needs a vector database (Pinecone, ChromaDB etc.)
❌ More infrastructure, more cost, more maintenance
The Biggest Risk of RAG for Resumes

RAG splits documents into chunks before storing them. A resume split into chunks looks like:


Chunk 1: "Mokshit Jain | mgjain@gmail.com"
Chunk 2: "Experience: 2 years Python, React"
Chunk 3: "Projects: E-commerce, Spotify Clone"
Chunk 4: "Education: B.Tech Computer Science"

When RAG retrieves only 2-3 chunks, the LLM misses the full picture — it might score based on incomplete information. Your current approach feeds the entire resume to the LLM which is far more accurate for evaluation.

Simple Decision Rule

Are you searching across MANY documents?     → Use RAG
Are you evaluating ONE document at a time?   → Use your current approach

Your system evaluates one resume at a time → your current approach is correct and better.

RAG is a tool for a different problem. Don't add complexity that doesn't serve you.

Complete Theory First — Understanding From Scratch
What is a Socket?

A socket is like a telephone.

Before you talk to someone:
  → You need a phone (socket)
  → You need their number (IP address)
  → You need a line (port)

Socket = endpoint for communication
         between two machines over a network
What is an IP Address and Port?

IP Address = House address of a computer
             Example: 127.0.0.1 (your own machine = localhost)

Port = Door number of that house
       Different programs use different doors
       Example: 8080, 5000, 65432

Together: IP:Port = exact destination
          127.0.0.1:8080
TCP vs UDP — The Core Difference

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Think of it like a PHONE CALL

→ Connection must be established first
→ Data arrives in ORDER
→ If packet is lost → it is RETRANSMITTED
→ Receiver sends ACKNOWLEDGEMENT (ACK)
→ Reliable but slightly slower
→ Used in: HTTP, email, file transfer

UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Think of it like POSTING A LETTER

→ No connection needed
→ Just send and forget
→ No guarantee of delivery
→ No guarantee of order
→ No acknowledgement
→ Faster but unreliable
→ Used in: video calls, gaming, live streaming
How TCP Connection Works — 3 Way Handshake

CLIENT                          SERVER
  │                               │
  │──── SYN (I want to connect) ─►│
  │                               │
  │◄─ SYN-ACK (OK, I'm ready) ───│
  │                               │
  │──── ACK (Great, let's talk) ─►│
  │                               │
  │    CONNECTION ESTABLISHED     │
  │                               │
  │◄──────── DATA ───────────────►│
Stop and Wait Protocol — Theory

The simplest reliable data transfer protocol.

Rule:
  Sender sends ONE packet
  Then WAITS for ACK before sending next packet
  If ACK not received within timeout → RETRANSMIT
  If ACK received → send next packet

Timeline:
  Sender: [Packet 0] ────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:           ◄──── [ACK 0] ──
  Sender: [Packet 1] ────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:           ◄──── [ACK 1] ──
  ...

Problem:
  Very slow — only ONE packet in transit at a time
  Wire is idle while waiting for ACK
  Efficiency = packet_size / (packet_size + 2*propagation_delay)
Go Back N Protocol — Theory

More efficient than Stop and Wait.

Key concepts:
  Window Size (N) = how many packets can be
                    sent WITHOUT waiting for ACK

  Sender can send N packets at a time
  Receiver only accepts IN-ORDER packets
  If packet i is lost → sender goes back
  and retransmits from packet i onwards
  (even if later packets were received correctly)

Timeline (Window=3):
  Sender: [0][1][2] ──────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:         ◄──── [ACK 0] ─────
  Sender: [3] ────────────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:         ◄──── [ACK 1] ─────
  Sender: [4] ────────────────────────► Receiver

  If packet [1] is LOST:
  Sender: [0][1][2] → 1 is lost
  Receiver gets 0 (ACK 0), discards 2 (out of order)
  Timer expires for 1
  Sender goes back → retransmits [1][2][3]...

Window size N means:
  Sequence numbers needed = N (0 to N-1)
Key Difference Between Stop-and-Wait and Go-Back-N

Stop and Wait:        Go Back N:
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Window size = 1       Window size = N
One packet at a time  N packets at a time
Very slow             Much faster
Simple                More complex
On loss: resend 1     On loss: resend N packets

# tcp_server.py
import socket

def start_tcp_server():
    HOST = '127.0.0.1'   # localhost
    PORT = 65432         # port to listen on

    # AF_INET = IPv4
    # SOCK_STREAM = TCP
    server_socket = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)

    # SO_REUSEADDR = allows reuse of port immediately after close
    server_socket.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)

    # bind = attach socket to this address and port
    server_socket.bind((HOST, PORT))

    # listen = start accepting connections, 5 = backlog queue size
    server_socket.listen(5)
    print(f"[TCP SERVER] Listening on {HOST}:{PORT}")

    # accept = wait until a client connects
    # returns new socket for this specific client + client address
    conn, addr = server_socket.accept()
    print(f"[TCP SERVER] Connected by {addr}")

    with conn:
        while True:
            # recv = receive data, 1024 = buffer size in bytes
            data = conn.recv(1024)
            if not data:
                break

            message = data.decode()
            print(f"[TCP SERVER] Received: {message}")

            # send acknowledgement back
            response = f"ACK: {message}"
            conn.sendall(response.encode())

    server_socket.close()
    print("[TCP SERVER] Connection closed")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    start_tcp_server()

import socket

def start_udp_server():
    HOST = '127.0.0.1'
    PORT = 65433

    # SOCK_DGRAM = UDP (no connection, just datagrams)
    server_socket = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    server_socket.bind((HOST, PORT))
    print(f"[UDP SERVER] Listening on {HOST}:{PORT}")

    while True:
        # recvfrom = receive data AND sender's address
        # UDP has no persistent connection so we need address each time
        data, addr = server_socket.recvfrom(1024)
        message = data.decode()
        print(f"[UDP SERVER] Received from {addr}: {message}")

        if message == "QUIT":
            print("[UDP SERVER] Shutting down")
            break

        response = f"ACK: {message}"
        # sendto = send to specific address (no connection maintained)
        server_socket.sendto(response.encode(), addr)

    server_socket.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    start_udp_server()

# stop_and_wait.py
import socket
import time
import random
import threading

# ─────────────────────────────────────────
# STOP AND WAIT SENDER
# ─────────────────────────────────────────
def stop_and_wait_sender(packets, loss_probability=0.2):
    """
    Simulates Stop and Wait sender.
    loss_probability = chance that a packet or ACK is "lost"
    """
    HOST = '127.0.0.1'
    PORT = 65434

    sender = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    sender.settimeout(2)   # 2 second timeout — if no ACK → retransmit

    print("\n[SENDER] Stop and Wait Protocol Started")
    print(f"[SENDER] Sending {len(packets)} packets")
    print("=" * 50)

    seq_num = 0   # sequence number alternates 0 and 1 in stop-and-wait

    for i, packet in enumerate(packets):
        message = f"SEQ:{seq_num}|DATA:{packet}"
        acknowledged = False

        while not acknowledged:
            # simulate packet loss

            if random.random() < loss_probability:
                print(f"[SENDER] Packet {seq_num} LOST in network (simulated)")
            else:
                print(f"[SENDER] Sent Packet {seq_num}: '{packet}'")
                sender.sendto(message.encode(), (HOST, PORT))

            try:
                # wait for ACK
                ack_data, _ = sender.recvfrom(1024)
                ack = ack_data.decode()
                ack_num = int(ack.split(":")[1])

                if ack_num == seq_num:
                    print(f"[SENDER] ACK {ack_num} received ✓")
                    acknowledged = True
                    seq_num = 1 - seq_num  # toggle 0→1 or 1→0
                else:
                    print(f"[SENDER] Wrong ACK {ack_num}, expected {seq_num}. Retransmitting...")

            except socket.timeout:
                print(f"[SENDER] TIMEOUT waiting for ACK {seq_num}. Retransmitting...")

        time.sleep(0.5)  # small delay between packets for readability

    # signal end
    sender.sendto("END".encode(), (HOST, PORT))
    sender.close()
    print("\n[SENDER] All packets sent successfully")

# ─────────────────────────────────────────
# STOP AND WAIT RECEIVER
# ─────────────────────────────────────────

def stop_and_wait_receiver(loss_probability=0.2):
    """
    Simulates Stop and Wait receiver.
    """
    HOST = '127.0.0.1'
    PORT = 65434

    receiver = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    receiver.bind((HOST, PORT))

    print("[RECEIVER] Stop and Wait Receiver Ready")

    expected_seq = 0
    received_packets = []

    while True:
        data, addr = receiver.recvfrom(1024)
        message = data.decode()

        if message == "END":
            print("[RECEIVER] All packets received successfully")

import socket
import time
import random
import threading

WINDOW_SIZE = 4       # N = 4 (sender can send 4 packets before waiting)
TIMEOUT = 2           # 2 seconds before retransmission
LOSS_PROB = 0.3       # 30% packet loss probability
HOST = '127.0.0.1'
PORT = 65435

# ─────────────────────────────────────────
# GO BACK N SENDER
# ─────────────────────────────────────────
def go_back_n_sender(packets):
    sender = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    sender.settimeout(TIMEOUT)

    total = len(packets)
    base = 0          # oldest unacknowledged packet
    next_seq = 0      # next packet to send
    ack_received = [False] * total

    print("\n[GBN SENDER] Go Back N Protocol Started")
    print(f"[GBN SENDER] Window Size = {WINDOW_SIZE}")
    print(f"[GBN SENDER] Total packets = {total}")
    print("=" * 50)

    while base < total:
        # send all packets within the window
        while next_seq < total and next_seq < base + WINDOW_SIZE:

            message = f"SEQ:{next_seq}|DATA:{packets[next_seq]}"

            if random.random() < LOSS_PROB:
                print(f"[GBN SENDER] Packet {next_seq} LOST (simulated)")
            else:
                print(f"[GBN SENDER] Sent Packet {next_seq}: '{packets[next_seq]}'  "
                      f"[Window: {base} to {min(base+WINDOW_SIZE-1, total-1)}]")
                sender.sendto(message.encode(), (HOST, PORT))

            next_seq += 1

        # wait for ACK
        try:
            ack_data, _ = sender.recvfrom(1024)
            ack_num = int(ack_data.decode().split(":")[1])
            print(f"[GBN SENDER] ACK {ack_num} received")

            # cumulative ACK — all packets up to ack_num are acknowledged
            if ack_num >= base:
                base = ack_num + 1
                print(f"[GBN SENDER] Window moves → base = {base}")

        except socket.timeout:
            # TIMEOUT → Go Back N → retransmit from base
            print(f"\n[GBN SENDER] TIMEOUT! Going back to packet {base}")
            print(f"[GBN SENDER] Retransmitting packets {base} to {next_seq-1}")
            next_seq = base   # reset next_seq to base → resend all window packets

        time.sleep(0.3)

    sender.sendto("END".encode(), (HOST, PORT))
    sender.close()

    print("\n[GBN SENDER] All packets acknowledged successfully")

# ─────────────────────────────────────────
# GO BACK N RECEIVER
# ─────────────────────────────────────────
def go_back_n_receiver(total_packets):
    receiver = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    receiver.bind((HOST, PORT))

    print("[GBN RECEIVER] Go Back N Receiver Ready")

    expected_seq = 0
    received = []

    while True:
        data, addr = receiver.recvfrom(1024)
        message = data.decode()

        if message == "END":
            break

        parts    = message.split("|")
        seq_num  = int(parts[0].split(":")[1])
        pkt_data = parts[1].split(":")[1]

        print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Received Packet {seq_num}: '{pkt_data}'")

        if seq_num == expected_seq:
            # in-order packet → accept it
            received.append(pkt_data)
            print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Packet {seq_num} ACCEPTED ✓")


            # send ACK
            ack = f"ACK:{seq_num}"
            receiver.sendto(ack.encode(), addr)
            print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Sent ACK {seq_num}")

            expected_seq += 1
        else:
            # out-of-order packet → DISCARD (Go Back N discards out-of-order)
            print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Packet {seq_num} DISCARDED "
                  f"(expected {expected_seq}) — out of order")

            # send ACK for last correctly received packet
            if expected_seq > 0:
                ack = f"ACK:{expected_seq - 1}"
                receiver.sendto(ack.encode(), addr)
                print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Sent ACK {expected_seq-1} (last good)")

    print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Final received data: {received}")
    receiver.close()

What is a Socket?

A socket is like a telephone.

Before you talk to someone:
  → You need a phone (socket)
  → You need their number (IP address)
  → You need a line (port)

Socket = endpoint for communication
         between two machines over a network
What is an IP Address and Port?

IP Address = House address of a computer
             Example: 127.0.0.1 (your own machine = localhost)

Port = Door number of that house
       Different programs use different doors
       Example: 8080, 5000, 65432

Together: IP:Port = exact destination
          127.0.0.1:8080
TCP vs UDP — The Core Difference

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Think of it like a PHONE CALL

→ Connection must be established first
→ Data arrives in ORDER
→ If packet is lost → it is RETRANSMITTED
→ Receiver sends ACKNOWLEDGEMENT (ACK)
→ Reliable but slightly slower
→ Used in: HTTP, email, file transfer

UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Think of it like POSTING A LETTER

→ No connection needed
→ Just send and forget
→ No guarantee of delivery
→ No guarantee of order
→ No acknowledgement
→ Faster but unreliable
→ Used in: video calls, gaming, live streaming
How TCP Connection Works — 3 Way Handshake

CLIENT                          SERVER
  │                               │
  │──── SYN (I want to connect) ─►│
  │                               │
  │◄─ SYN-ACK (OK, I'm ready) ───│
  │                               │
  │──── ACK (Great, let's talk) ─►│
  │                               │
  │    CONNECTION ESTABLISHED     │
  │                               │
  │◄──────── DATA ───────────────►│
Stop and Wait Protocol — Theory

The simplest reliable data transfer protocol.

Rule:
  Sender sends ONE packet
  Then WAITS for ACK before sending next packet
  If ACK not received within timeout → RETRANSMIT
  If ACK received → send next packet

Timeline:
  Sender: [Packet 0] ────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:           ◄──── [ACK 0] ──
  Sender: [Packet 1] ────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:           ◄──── [ACK 1] ──
  ...

Problem:
  Very slow — only ONE packet in transit at a time
  Wire is idle while waiting for ACK
  Efficiency = packet_size / (packet_size + 2*propagation_delay)
Go Back N Protocol — Theory

More efficient than Stop and Wait.

Key concepts:
  Window Size (N) = how many packets can be
                    sent WITHOUT waiting for ACK

  Sender can send N packets at a time
  Receiver only accepts IN-ORDER packets
  If packet i is lost → sender goes back
  and retransmits from packet i onwards
  (even if later packets were received correctly)

Timeline (Window=3):
  Sender: [0][1][2] ──────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:         ◄──── [ACK 0] ─────
  Sender: [3] ────────────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:         ◄──── [ACK 1] ─────
  Sender: [4] ────────────────────────► Receiver

  If packet [1] is LOST:
  Sender: [0][1][2] → 1 is lost
  Receiver gets 0 (ACK 0), discards 2 (out of order)
  Timer expires for 1
  Sender goes back → retransmits [1][2][3]...

Window size N means:
  Sequence numbers needed = N (0 to N-1)
Key Difference Between Stop-and-Wait and Go-Back-N

Stop and Wait:        Go Back N:
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Window size = 1       Window size = N
One packet at a time  N packets at a time
Very slow             Much faster
Simple                More complex
On loss: resend 1     On loss: resend N packets

import socket

def start_tcp_server():
    HOST = '127.0.0.1'   # localhost
    PORT = 65432         # port to listen on

    # AF_INET = IPv4
    # SOCK_STREAM = TCP
    server_socket = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)

    # SO_REUSEADDR = allows reuse of port immediately after close
    server_socket.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)

    # bind = attach socket to this address and port
    server_socket.bind((HOST, PORT))

    # listen = start accepting connections, 5 = backlog queue size
    server_socket.listen(5)
    print(f"[TCP SERVER] Listening on {HOST}:{PORT}")

    # accept = wait until a client connects
    # returns new socket for this specific client + client address
    conn, addr = server_socket.accept()
    print(f"[TCP SERVER] Connected by {addr}")

    with conn:
        while True:
            # recv = receive data, 1024 = buffer size in bytes
            data = conn.recv(1024)
            if not data:
                break

            message = data.decode()
            print(f"[TCP SERVER] Received: {message}")

            # send acknowledgement back
            response = f"ACK: {message}"
            conn.sendall(response.encode())

    server_socket.close()
    print("[TCP SERVER] Connection closed")

    print(f"[SENDER] Sending {len(packets)} packets")
    print("=" * 50)

    seq_num = 0   # sequence number alternates 0 and 1 in stop-and-wait

    for i, packet in enumerate(packets):
        message = f"SEQ:{seq_num}|DATA:{packet}"
        acknowledged = False

        while not acknowledged:
            # simulate packet loss

            if random.random() < loss_probability:
                print(f"[SENDER] Packet {seq_num} LOST in network (simulated)")
            else:
                print(f"[SENDER] Sent Packet {seq_num}: '{packet}'")
                sender.sendto(message.encode(), (HOST, PORT))

                ack = ack_data.decode()

                    seq_num = 1 - seq_num  # toggle 0→1 or 1→0
                else:
                    print(f"[SENDER] Wrong ACK {ack_num}, expected {seq_num}. Retransmitting...")

            except socket.timeout:
                print(f"[SENDER] TIMEOUT waiting for ACK {seq_num}. Retransmitting...")

import socket
import time
import random
import threading

WINDOW_SIZE = 4       # N = 4 (sender can send 4 packets before waiting)
TIMEOUT = 2           # 2 seconds before retransmission
LOSS_PROB = 0.3       # 30% packet loss probability
HOST = '127.0.0.1'
PORT = 65435

# ─────────────────────────────────────────
# GO BACK N SENDER
# ─────────────────────────────────────────
def go_back_n_sender(packets):
    sender = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    sender.settimeout(TIMEOUT)

    total = len(packets)
    base = 0          # oldest unacknowledged packet
    next_seq = 0      # next packet to send
    ack_received = [False] * total

    print("\n[GBN SENDER] Go Back N Protocol Started")
    print(f"[GBN SENDER] Window Size = {WINDOW_SIZE}")
    print(f"[GBN SENDER] Total packets = {total}")
    print("=" * 50)

    while base < total:
        # send all packets within the window
        while next_seq < total and next_seq < base + WINDOW_SIZE:

            message = f"SEQ:{next_seq}|DATA:{packets[next_seq]}"

            if random.random() < LOSS_PROB:
                print(f"[GBN SENDER] Packet {next_seq} LOST (simulated)")
            else:
                print(f"[GBN SENDER] Sent Packet {next_seq}: '{packets[next_seq]}'  "
                      f"[Window: {base} to {min(base+WINDOW_SIZE-1, total-1)}]")
                sender.sendto(message.encode(), (HOST, PORT))

            next_seq += 1

        # wait for ACK
        try:
            ack_data, _ = sender.recvfrom(1024)
            ack_num = int(ack_data.decode().split(":")[1])
            print(f"[GBN SENDER] ACK {ack_num} received")

            # cumulative ACK — all packets up to ack_num are acknowledged
            if ack_num >= base:
                base = ack_num + 1
                print(f"[GBN SENDER] Window moves → base = {base}")

        except socket.timeout:
            # TIMEOUT → Go Back N → retransmit from base
            print(f"\n[GBN SENDER] TIMEOUT! Going back to packet {base}")
            print(f"[GBN SENDER] Retransmitting packets {base} to {next_seq-1}")
            next_seq = base   # reset next_seq to base → resend all window packets

        time.sleep(0.3)

    sender.sendto("END".encode(), (HOST, PORT))
    sender.close()

    print("\n[GBN SENDER] All packets acknowledged successfully")

# ─────────────────────────────────────────
# GO BACK N RECEIVER
# ─────────────────────────────────────────
def go_back_n_receiver(total_packets):
    receiver = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    receiver.bind((HOST, PORT))

    print("[GBN RECEIVER] Go Back N Receiver Ready")

    expected_seq = 0
    received = []

    while True:
        data, addr = receiver.recvfrom(1024)
        message = data.decode()

        if message == "END":
            break

        parts    = message.split("|")
        seq_num  = int(parts[0].split(":")[1])
        pkt_data = parts[1].split(":")[1]

        print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Received Packet {seq_num}: '{pkt_data}'")

        if seq_num == expected_seq:
            # in-order packet → accept it
            received.append(pkt_data)
            print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Packet {seq_num} ACCEPTED ✓")


            # send ACK
            ack = f"ACK:{seq_num}"
            receiver.sendto(ack.encode(), addr)
            print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Sent ACK {seq_num}")

            expected_seq += 1
        else:
            # out-of-order packet → DISCARD (Go Back N discards out-of-order)
            print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Packet {seq_num} DISCARDED "
                  f"(expected {expected_seq}) — out of order")

            # send ACK for last correctly received packet
            if expected_seq > 0:
                ack = f"ACK:{expected_seq - 1}"
                receiver.sendto(ack.encode(), addr)
                print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Sent ACK {expected_seq-1} (last good)")

    print(f"[GBN RECEIVER] Final received data: {received}")
    receiver.close()

               "Packet_D", "Packet_E", "Packet_F",
               "Packet_G", "Packet_H"]

    receiver_thread = threading.Thread(
        target=go_back_n_receiver,
        args=(len(packets),),
        daemon=True

    )
    receiver_thread.start()

TCP vs UDP — The Core Difference

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)

UDP (User Datagram Protocol)
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

→ Faster but unreliable

How TCP Connection Works — 3 Way Handshake

CLIENT                          SERVER
  │                               │
  │──── SYN (I want to connect) ─►│
  │                               │
  │◄─ SYN-ACK (OK, I'm ready) ───│
  │                               │
  │──── ACK (Great, let's talk) ─►│
  │                               │
  │    CONNECTION ESTABLISHED     │
  │                               │
  │◄──────── DATA ───────────────►│
Stop and Wait Protocol — Theory

The simplest reliable data transfer protocol.

Rule:
  Sender sends ONE packet
  Then WAITS for ACK before sending next packet
  If ACK not received within timeout → RETRANSMIT
  If ACK received → send next packet

Timeline:
  Sender: [Packet 0] ────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:           ◄──── [ACK 0] ──
  Sender: [Packet 1] ────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:           ◄──── [ACK 1] ──
  ...

Problem:
  Very slow — only ONE packet in transit at a time
  Wire is idle while waiting for ACK
  Efficiency = packet_size / (packet_size + 2*propagation_delay)
Go Back N Protocol — Theory

More efficient than Stop and Wait.

Key concepts:
  Window Size (N) = how many packets can be
                    sent WITHOUT waiting for ACK

  Sender can send N packets at a time
  Receiver only accepts IN-ORDER packets
  If packet i is lost → sender goes back
  and retransmits from packet i onwards
  (even if later packets were received correctly)

Timeline (Window=3):
  Sender: [0][1][2] ──────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:         ◄──── [ACK 0] ─────
  Sender: [3] ────────────────────────► Receiver
  Receiver:         ◄──── [ACK 1] ─────
  Sender: [4] ────────────────────────► Receiver

  If packet [1] is LOST:
  Sender: [0][1][2] → 1 is lost
  Receiver gets 0 (ACK 0), discards 2 (out of order)
  Timer expires for 1
  Sender goes back → retransmits [1][2][3]...

Window size N means:
  Sequence numbers needed = N (0 to N-1)

    server_socket.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)

    conn, addr = server_socket.accept()
    print(f"[TCP SERVER] Connected by {addr}")

            data = conn.recv(1024)
            if not data:

            print(f"[TCP SERVER] Received: {message}")

            # send acknowledgement back

    print(f"[GBN SENDER] Window Size = {WINDOW_SIZE}")
    print(f"[GBN SENDER] Total packets = {total}")
    print("=" * 50)

        while next_seq < total and next_seq < base + WINDOW_SIZE:

            message = f"SEQ:{next_seq}|DATA:{packets[next_seq]}"

            if random.random() < LOSS_PROB:
                print(f"[GBN SENDER] Packet {next_seq} LOST (simulated)")

                      f"[Window: {base} to {min(base+WINDOW_SIZE-1, total-1)}]")
                sender.sendto(message.encode(), (HOST, PORT))

import random, time, threading
from typing import Callable, Optional

scapy.all protocol classes (IP, TCP, UDP, ICMP, DNS, DNSQR, DNSRR, Ether, Raw) — these are Scapy's packet layer classes. This is the core Scapy idiom: you build a packet by stacking layers with /, e.g.

python
IP(src=src_ip, dst=dst_ip) / TCP(sport=src_port, dport=dst_port, flags="PA") / Raw(load=http_payload.encode())

reads as "an IP packet, containing a TCP segment, containing a raw payload" — each / nests the next layer inside the previous one's payload, exactly like real packet encapsulation (Ethernet → IP → TCP → data). Raw wraps arbitrary bytes when Scapy doesn't have a dedicated class for the payload (here, literal HTTP text or fake TLS bytes). Note Ether and IPv6 are imported but never actually used in this file — more small dead imports worth cleaning up.

Class constants COMMON_DOMAINS, INTERNAL_SUBNET, EXTERNAL_IPS — just realistic-looking fixture data so generated packets resemble real traffic (Google, GitHub, Cloudflare IPs) rather than obviously-fake 1.2.3.4 addresses.

generate_random_ip(internal) — if internal=True, builds a 192.168.1.x address (private LAN range, per RFC 1918) using an f-string; otherwise builds a fully random public-looking IP. This is why later generate_http_packet() calls it with internal=True for the source (simulating "your laptop") and picks from EXTERNAL_IPS for the destination (simulating "the internet").

generate_http_packet() / generate_https_packet() / generate_dns_packet() / generate_icmp_packet() — each builds one realistic packet for that protocol:

HTTP: crafts a literal HTTP request string ("GET /path HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: ...\r\n\r\n") and stuffs it in as the TCP payload — flags="PA" means PSH+ACK, a normal mid-conversation TCP packet.
HTTPS: fakes a TLS handshake byte prefix (\x16\x03\x01... — the real TLS record header for a Handshake message) followed by random.randbytes(...) to simulate opaque encrypted data (since real HTTPS payloads are unreadable anyway, random bytes are a faithful stand-in).
DNS: random.random() > 0.4 branches into either a query (rd=1 = recursion desired, qd=DNSQR(...) = one question record) or a response (qr=1 = this is a response, aa=1 = authoritative answer, plus an an=DNSRR(...) answer record) — modeling both halves of a real DNS exchange.
ICMP: type=8 is Echo Request (ping), type=0 is Echo Reply — the real ICMP type codes from RFC 792.

generate_port_scan_packet() / generate_syn_flood_packet() — these simulate attack traffic for testing downstream threat-detection: a lone TCP SYN (flags="S") to a target port models a scanner probing if a port is open; the SYN flood additionally uses generate_random_ip(internal=False) as a spoofed source, modeling how real SYN-flood DoS attacks fake their origin.

generate_random_packet() — a weighted random dispatcher using cumulative probability bands (r < 0.35 → HTTPS, r < 0.60 → HTTP, etc.), so the traffic mix looks like real-world proportions (lots of HTTPS/HTTP, a little DNS, rare attack packets) rather than uniform noise.

start_simulation(packets_per_second, total_packets):


python
def _worker():
    interval = 1.0 / max(1.0, packets_per_second)
    while self.is_running:
        pkt = self.generate_random_packet()
        ...
        if self.packet_callback:
            try: self.packet_callback(pkt)
            except Exception: pass
        ...
        time.sleep(interval)

self._thread = threading.Thread(target=_worker, daemon=True)
self._thread.start()
interval = 1.0 / pps — converts "packets per second" into "seconds to sleep between packets" (basic rate limiting).
The callback is wrapped in try/except Exception: pass deliberately — a bug in whatever's consuming the packet (e.g., the CLI renderer) must never crash the packet-generation thread.
daemon=True — marks the thread as a daemon, meaning Python won't wait for it before exiting the whole process; important so a forgotten simulator thread doesn't hang your program on exit.

stop_simulation() — flips the flag the while self.is_running loop is checking, then self._thread.join(timeout=1.0) waits (up to 1s) for the thread to actually finish before returning, so callers can be sure the thread is really stopped, not just "asked nicely."

collections.deque — a double-ended queue. Critically, deque(maxlen=N) auto-evicts the oldest item once it hits capacity — this is exactly how the "ring buffer (10k packets)" mentioned in your README is implemented: no manual trimming logic needed, deque does it natively and efficiently (O(1) append/pop from either end, unlike a plain list which is O(n) to pop from the front).
collections.Counter — a dict subclass specialized for counting things; self.protocol_counts["TCP"] += 1 "just works" even the first time (defaults missing keys to 0), which is why it's used for the protocol breakdown.
pydantic.Field — like BaseModel before, but Field(default_factory=dict) is needed instead of a bare = {} default because mutable defaults are a classic Python footgun — a bare {} default would be shared across every CaptureStats instance; default_factory makes Pydantic call dict() fresh for each new instance.
scapy.all.AsyncSniffer — Scapy's non-blocking sniffer class (from the README: it captures on a background thread and calls your prn callback per packet).
Packet — the base type for all Scapy packets, used purely as a type hint (Callable[[Packet], None]).
Relative imports of InterfaceManager and TrafficSimulator — this file is the composition point: it doesn't know how to list interfaces or how to fake packets, it just orchestrates the two other modules.

class CaptureStats(BaseModel): — a pure snapshot/DTO (data transfer object) of engine state at one instant: totals, rates, protocol breakdown, running/paused flags, which interface/filter is active, and whether it's simulated. This is what cli.py (and eventually a web API) reads to render — the engine itself is never rendered directly, only its CaptureStats snapshot.

class PacketCaptureEngine.__init__:


python
self._buffer: deque = deque(maxlen=max_buffer_size)
self._lock = threading.Lock()
self._subscribers: List[Callable[[Packet], None]] = []
self._rate_window: deque = deque(maxlen=1000)
self._lock — a mutex. It exists because packets arrive on a different thread (the sniffer's or simulator's background thread) than whatever thread calls get_stats() or get_buffered_packets() (e.g., the CLI's main loop). Without the lock, two threads mutating/reading self._buffer/self.total_packets simultaneously could corrupt state or throw RuntimeError: deque mutated during iteration.
self._subscribers — this is the observer pattern: other parts of NetSleuth (future phases — parser, rule engine, AI models) can call add_subscriber(fn) to get a live feed of every packet, without the capture engine needing to know anything about them.
self._rate_window — a separate bounded deque of (timestamp, packet_length) tuples, kept apart from the main packet buffer specifically to compute packets/bytes-per-second without re-scanning the whole 10,000-packet buffer every time.

add_subscriber / remove_subscriber — straightforward list management, with an if callback not in self._subscribers guard to prevent duplicate registration.

_classify_protocol(pkt):


python
if pkt.haslayer(DNS): return "DNS"
elif pkt.haslayer(TCP):
    sport, dport = pkt[TCP].sport, pkt[TCP].dport
    if sport == 80 or dport == 80: return "HTTP"
    elif sport == 443 or dport == 443: return "HTTPS"
    return "TCP"
elif pkt.haslayer(UDP): ...
elif pkt.haslayer(ICMP): return "ICMP"
elif pkt.haslayer(ARP): return "ARP"
return "OTHER"

pkt.haslayer(X) is Scapy's way of asking "does this packet contain a layer of type X anywhere in its stack?" and pkt[TCP] extracts that layer to read its fields. The order matters: DNS is checked before TCP/UDP because DNS can ride on either transport, so checking it first avoids DNS packets getting misclassified as plain "UDP". Port 80/443 checks approximate protocol-by-port (a real classifier would eventually want deeper inspection, but port-based heuristics are the standard first pass).

_on_packet_received(pkt) — the callback registered with both the sniffer and the simulator. This is the single choke point all captured packets pass through, live or simulated:


python
if not self.is_running or self.is_paused:
    return

This early-return is why pause() doesn't actually stop the sniffer thread — the sniffer keeps calling this function, but it becomes a no-op while paused, which is cheaper/simpler than actually stopping and restarting a live socket capture.



with self._lock:
    self.total_packets += 1
    self.total_bytes += pkt_len
    ...
    self._buffer.append(pkt)
    self._rate_window.append((now, pkt_len))

Everything that touches shared state happens inside the lock. Then, outside the lock:


python
for subscriber in self._subscribers:
    try: subscriber(pkt)
    except Exception: pass

Subscribers are called after releasing the lock — important, because if a subscriber's callback were slow or itself tried to call back into the engine (e.g., engine.get_stats()), holding the lock during that call could deadlock or badly stall the capture thread. The try/except again ensures one broken subscriber can't kill packet capture for everyone else.

Building kwargs conditionally (rather than always passing iface=None, filter=None) avoids passing spurious Nones into Scapy's constructor. store=False matches what the README explained — don't let Scapy accumulate every packet internally too (we have our own deque for that; storing twice would waste memory). The whole point of this try/except is the "NetSleuth Fallback Architecture" from your README: opening a raw socket without root raises PermissionError/OSError, and instead of crashing, it transparently swaps to _start_simulation() — this is the key design decision that lets the entire rest of the pipeline (parser, dashboard, tests, CI) run without ever needing sudo.

pause() / resume() — just flip is_paused; as noted, actual filtering happens in _on_packet_received's early return.

stop():


python
if self._sniffer and self._sniffer.running:
    try: self._sniffer.stop()
    except Exception: pass
    self._sniffer = None
if self._simulator:
    self._simulator.stop_simulation()
    self._simulator = None

Cleans up whichever one is active — checks .running first because calling .stop() on an already-stopped sniffer can raise; wrapped in try/except as one more defensive layer; nulling out the references afterward lets Python's garbage collector reclaim the thread objects and lets start() be called again cleanly later.

get_stats() — the most subtle method:


python
now = time.time()
window_cutoff = now - 1.5
with self._lock:
    recent_entries = [entry for entry in self._rate_window if entry[0] >= window_cutoff]
    while self._rate_window and self._rate_window[0][0] < (now - 5.0):
        self._rate_window.popleft()
    window_duration = max(0.5, (now - recent_entries[0][0])) if recent_entries else 1.0
    pps = len(recent_entries) / window_duration if recent_entries else 0.0
    bps = sum(entry[1] for entry in recent_entries) / window_duration if recent_entries else 0.0

This computes a sliding-window rate rather than an all-time average, so "packets/sec" reflects recent activity, not activity since the capture started an hour ago. It filters _rate_window down to the last 1.5 seconds for the actual rate calculation, but separately prunes anything older than 5 seconds from the deque itself (a lazy garbage-collection pass, done here rather than on every single packet arrival, to keep _on_packet_received as fast as possible). max(0.5, ...) guards against division by a near-zero duration when very few packets have arrived (which would otherwise make the rate spike to an absurd number).

get_buffered_packets(limit) / clear_buffer() — straightforward reads/resets, both properly wrapped in with self._lock.

  → imports cli.py
